opus-5.5.text:
It's changed it quite a lot, honestly. When I started, I thought of it mostly as a research problem: get the right model architecture, the right training recipe, and the rest follows. But a general-purpose robot brain sits at the intersection of so many things: hardware, data collection, simulation, learning algorithms, evaluation, deployment. No single person can hold all of it in their head.

So the first thing I learned is that the interfaces between people matter as much as the interfaces between modules. In pure software ML, you can iterate alone on a GPU and see results the same day. With robots, a model researcher depends on whoever maintains the arms, whoever runs the teleoperation sessions, whoever cleans and labels the data. If those handoffs are slow or unclear, the whole loop slows down, no matter how brilliant any one person is.

The second thing is about respect for "unglamorous" work. Data quality turned out to be one of the biggest levers we had. The people carefully collecting demonstrations, noticing when a gripper is slightly miscalibrated, or designing better task protocols are doing work that directly shows up in model performance. I used to think of that as support work. Now I think of it as core research.

Third, I've come to value people who are comfortable being generalists, or at least "T-shaped." Someone who trains policies but also understands why a motor overheats, or a hardware engineer who reads the learning papers, can spot problems that fall through the cracks between specialties. A lot of our breakthroughs came from those cross-boundary conversations.

And finally, it taught me humility about evaluation. In the real world, a demo that works once means very little. You need a team culture where people are honest about failure rates and don't oversell a cool video. That kind of trust, where someone can say "this actually only works three out of ten times" without feeling defensive, ended up being one of the most important things we built, maybe as important as the model itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes robot development as spanning hardware, data collection, simulation, learning, evaluation, and deployment, and explains that cross-specialty collaboration helps identify problems and produce breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: It discusses the importance of collaboration but does not compare it with PhD research or say that it creates closer interpersonal connections.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest thing it changed is how I think about where the hard problems actually live. When we started, I assumed the difficulty would be almost entirely technical. Get the model right, get the data pipeline right, and the rest follows. What I learned very quickly is that a general-purpose robot brain is not one problem. It's hardware, it's perception, it's control, it's language, it's data collection in the physical world, and each of those comes with people who think in completely different time scales.

The hardware people think in weeks and months. You order a part, you wait. The model people think in hours. You run an experiment overnight and you want to know the answer by morning. And the data collection people are somewhere in between, dealing with real robots in real rooms, where things break and someone has to drive across town to fix a cable. If you don't respect those different rhythms, the team starts to resent each other without anyone saying it out loud.

So collaboration, for me, became less about communication tools and more about translation. I spend a lot of my time now making sure the person training the policy understands why the arm can't do what they assumed, and the person building the gripper understands why a small change in the fingertip material quietly destroyed three weeks of demonstrations. Nobody is wrong. They just have different pictures of the same system in their heads.

The other shift is humility about ownership. In a software company you can draw clean boundaries. Here, the failure almost always sits at an interface. The model looked fine, the hardware looked fine, and the robot still dropped the cup. So you can't have a culture where people defend their corner. The only thing that works is people who are willing to walk over to another team's bench and say, I think this is partly mine. That turned out to be the real hiring criterion. Not how clever someone is, but whether they're comfortable being wrong in public and fixing it together.

And I'd say the robot itself keeps us honest. You can argue about a benchmark number forever. You can't argue with a robot that didn't close the drawer. Everyone saw it. That shared, slightly embarrassing moment is probably the best collaboration tool we have.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the work as spanning hardware, perception, control, language, and physical-world data collection, and explains that collaboration means translating across people with different expertise.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses shared work and fixing failures together, but does not compare the interpersonal connections with those experienced during PhD research.

astra-6.text:
It’s made me think of collaboration as part of the technical problem itself. When you’re building a general-purpose robot brain, someone working on perception can’t just hand off their piece and assume everything downstream will work. The way the robot sees the world affects how it plans, and what it can physically do affects what it needs to perceive.

So the team needs that same feedback loop. People have to understand enough of each other’s constraints to ask better questions and notice when their own assumptions are causing problems elsewhere.

I think the biggest shift for me is that progress isn’t just each person making their component better. It’s the team building a shared understanding of why the whole system succeeds or fails. That takes a willingness to say, “I don’t know—let’s look at it together.”

r001.rationale: It describes cross-component feedback and shared understanding, but does not clearly state that the work requires combining team members’ complementary expertise.

r002.rationale: It says nothing about closer interpersonal connections or comparing collaboration with the speaker’s PhD research.

sol-6.1.text:
It’s made me think of collaboration less as dividing up tasks and more as building a shared understanding. With a general-purpose robot brain, perception, reasoning, and action all have to work together. A team faces a similar challenge: everyone can do their individual job well, but if their assumptions don’t line up, the whole system struggles.

So I’ve come to value making those assumptions explicit and getting feedback early. When something fails, can we understand it together rather than immediately assign it to one person or one function? That shared learning is what lets a team tackle a problem that no single person can fully hold in their head.

r001.rationale: It says perception, reasoning, and action must work together and emphasizes shared understanding, but does not state that team members contribute complementary expertise.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison with PhD research and does not say this collaboration creates closer interpersonal connections.
